A refrigerator keeps food cold by using a continuous cycle of evaporation and condensation to move heat from the inside of the unit to the outside. A refrigerant fluid flows through coils, absorbing heat from the air inside the fridge as it evaporates into a gas. This gas is then compressed by a compressor, which increases its temperature and pressure, and then flows through outdoor coils where it releases that heat into the surrounding room and condenses back into a liquid. This cycle repeats, effectively "pumping" heat out of the refrigerator to maintain a low internal temperature.

A refrigerator works by removing heat from its interior and releasing it into the surrounding air. A system of coils circulates a refrigerant—a substance that evaporates at a very low temperature—through the unit. As the liquid refrigerant flows through the evaporator coils inside the fridge, it absorbs heat from the food, causing it to turn into a gas. This gas then flows to the condenser coils on the outside, where it releases that heat into the room and cools back into a liquid. This continuous cycle keeps the inside of the refrigerator much cooler than the air outside.

A refrigerator works by removing heat from its interior and releasing it into the surrounding air. A system of coils circulates a refrigerant—a substance that evaporates at a very low temperature—through the unit. As the liquid refrigerant flows through the evaporator coils inside the fridge, it absorbs heat from the food, causing it to turn into a gas. This gas then flows to the condenser coils on the outside, where it releases that heat into the room and cools back into a liquid. This continuous cycle keeps the inside of the refrigerator much cooler than the air outside.

A refrigerator keeps food cold by using a continuous cycle of evaporation and condensation to move heat from the inside of the unit to the outside. A refrigerant fluid flows through coils, absorbing heat from the interior and turning into a gas. This gas is then compressed by a compressor, which increases its temperature and pressure. As the hot gas flows through condenser coils on the outside of the fridge, it releases its heat into the surrounding air and cools back into a liquid. Finally, the liquid passes through an expansion valve, where it cools rapidly before returning to the interior coils to repeat the process.
